The rule predicts success in both cases it was built to prevent. The find<-read_page row rests on the only find call and only read_page call in the corpus (1-of-1). All six signatures trace to ONE session file, not three. Central premise contradicted by the traces. Proposal asserted 'the pane is the failure point, not the API' with a budget of one browser call after a timeout, but trace 1 shows get_page_text AND javascript_tool both succeeding on the same tab immediately after a computer{scroll} timeout — the budget rule would have evicted the agent from a browser that was working. The headline 'ironclad' counterfactual (trace 4: screenshot burned 30s and taught nothing) is refuted by trace 5, where the agent returned and attempted another screenshot between edits: that is a verification loop, not a wasted call; the proposal could not distinguish 'confirmation was not decisive' from 'agent gave up because confirmation failed'. Rule 3 ('a screenshot is the worst post-timeout call') would train toward signature f05eda3928, which requires a screenshot before coordinate scroll — net negative from evidence in the same file. Misfire cost (shipping an unverified UI change on a transiently slow pane) exceeds the author's own stated ceiling of ~60s wall-clock per session. No retry storm occurred; user_corrections is empty.

Apparent cluster, dissolves on inspection. The three 'Command timed out after 2m 0s' entries look like a cross-signature pattern but are all the SAME session (f271523b) and have three unrelated root causes: (1) grep -oiE with unanchored .{0,45} context on a minified JSON file (backtracking), (2) a self-authored 90s watchdog subshell whose kill -9 did not reach the child, (3) a curl poll against a local fleet server on 127.0.0.1:8796 that hung. No single rule prevents all three, and each is a distinct one-off authoring bug rather than a property of the tool. The fourth signature (blocked sleep-then-cat) is a harness guard that already prints the exact remedy ('use Monitor with an until-loop / run_in_background') in the error text, and the agent complied on the next call.

reason: Not friction — observer false positive, and the candidate rule would be actively harmful. These 14 signatures share one shape: the agent batches independent diagnostic probes into one Bash call with 'echo === section ===' separators, and a sub-probe whose failure IS the informative result (an ls/cat on a file that is supposed to be absent) marks the whole call is_error=true. This is the only cluster this window spanning >=2 projects and >=2 sessions, so it was the one candidate that could clear the evidence bar. Transcript cf7cee31 refutes it outright: at idx 922 the agent read the exit-1 and wrote verbatim 'the `ls` exit code 1 is expected - the files correctly don't exist'; at idx 1175 it read an identical exit-1 and concluded '76 passed, zero leaks' and moved on. Real failures inside the same idiom (idx 1156, 6 pytest failures) were diagnosed correctly on the very next call. Zero retries, zero wrong conclusions, zero user corrections. The natural rule ('append || true / separate with ; so an expected absence does not fail the call') would train every future session to mask Bash exit codes, suppressing real failures - misfire cost far exceeds a cosmetic exit code the agent already reads correctly. The defect is in observe.py trusting is_error, not in agent behavior; recorded as a recommendation to the human rather than applied, per the standing rule that this loop does not unilaterally rewrite the miner that grades its own cycles.

Transient upstream infrastructure, not tooling friction. Both are 'claude-sonnet-5 is temporarily unavailable, so auto mode cannot determine the safety of Bash' from one session, and the error text already carries complete remediation ('Wait briefly and then try this action again... continue with other tasks that don't require this action'). Nothing a local skill or CLAUDE.md rule can prevent or improve on; the harness message is better-targeted than any rule we could write.

One conversation lineage, not two, and the harness block improved the outcome. The two occurrences are session f271523b (README.md, idx 2649-2653) and 47fc07e6 — but 47fc07e6's project dir is /private/tmp/claude-505/-Users-phil/f271523b-.../scratchpad/cheatdemo, i.e. a fleet worker spawned by the first session; distinct_projects:2 is an artifact of the tmp-dir naming scheme. Both recovered on the very next turn (Read then Write) at a cost of 2 tool calls each; zero wrong outcomes, zero user corrections. In the README case the forced Read was a net WIN: the blind first Write silently dropped the repo's load-bearing no-credentials blockquote, and the post-Read Write restored it verbatim — a rule making blind overwrite smoother would have cost something here. The instruction already exists in the Write tool description ('Overwriting an existing file you haven't Read will fail'), in the error text itself, and in the mechanical harness gate; a CLAUDE.md line is a fourth copy of text the model obeys on 88 of 90 Writes. Misfire cost is real: any 'Read before Write' rule fires on every new-file creation and generated artifact, the majority of Writes, nudging toward Reads of files that do not exist. Three further transcripts matching the error string (fdf69b01, 7982a36b, ba801a7c) contain ZERO real occurrences — verified by parsing for is_error tool_results — they are self-improve cycle sessions quoting observations.json; observe.py correctly excluded them.
